questions.prompt: What is naive intervention in this chapter?
choices: Any action that changes a system
Help that removes visible pain while increasing hidden fragility or blocking learning
Leaving a system alone no matter what

explanation.gentle: The chapter targets intervention that calms the surface while making the system less adaptive.
explanation.direct: Naive intervention is surface help that suppresses feedback and shifts harm into a less visible later form.
explanation.competitive: It is the fix that looks merciful now because it is sending the bill into hiding.

questions.prompt: Why can visible pain sometimes matter in the chapter's logic?
choices: Because pain is always good for growth
Because visible discomfort can carry signal about what needs correction
Because systems should never be made calmer

explanation.gentle: Some discomfort is information, not just a nuisance to erase.
explanation.direct: Visible pain can matter because it may be feedback that helps the system adapt before hidden damage accumulates.
explanation.competitive: The sting can be the alarm. Killing the alarm is not the same as removing the fire.

questions.prompt: What makes intervention harmful rather than helpful here?
choices: It suppresses corrective feedback and delays the real damage
It changes too many people at once
It relies on written rules

explanation.gentle: The chapter focuses on help that blocks the system from learning.
explanation.direct: Intervention becomes harmful when it removes the signal a system needed and turns small visible trouble into larger delayed trouble.
explanation.competitive: The fix goes bad when it stops cheap correction and starts financing a nastier future failure.

questions.prompt: Mira keeps stepping in every time her team hits a minor snag so nobody feels friction. Which response best fits the chapter?
choices: Keep rescuing every issue because calm always proves improvement
Let every problem explode to teach toughness
Reduce only the harms that threaten the team while keeping enough local feedback for people to learn

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants help that protects without erasing all learning.
explanation.direct: The best fit is intervention that limits serious damage while preserving corrective feedback instead of rescuing every small issue.
explanation.competitive: Do not buy a frictionless dashboard by bankrupting the team's ability to adjust.

questions.prompt: Which statement would the chapter reject most strongly?
choices: If discomfort disappears immediately, the intervention must have improved the system
Some intervention is necessary when exposures are too large to absorb safely
Useful help can preserve learning while limiting damage

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that calmer surfaces can hide worse structures underneath.
explanation.direct: Immediate relief does not prove real improvement because surface calm may come from blocking signal rather than fixing causes.
explanation.competitive: That answer mistakes quieter symptoms for a solved system.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's limit on its own critique?
choices: All intervention should be replaced by passivity
Pain should be preserved even when it threatens real damage
Some intervention still helps when it prevents ruin without destroying adaptive feedback

explanation.gentle: The chapter is not against help in general.
explanation.direct: Taleb's limit is that intervention can be useful when it protects the system from ruin while keeping learning and correction alive where possible.
explanation.competitive: The issue is not helping. It is whether the help saves the system without making it blind.

questions.prompt: A school installs a policy that suppresses every small attendance warning so reports look calmer, then absentee problems grow harder to detect. What pattern does this show?
choices: Healthy intervention reducing real fragility
Signal suppression creating delayed hidden harm
Prediction improving discipline

explanation.gentle: The system hid the warning signs instead of improving the underlying problem.
explanation.direct: This matches naive intervention: visible trouble went down because feedback was suppressed, not because fragility was reduced.
explanation.competitive: The report got prettier by teaching the system to stop seeing its own problem.

questions.prompt: Why can overhelping in personal life fit this chapter?
choices: Because all support weakens people
Because solving every small discomfort can block the other person's chance to adapt and self-correct
Because distance is always more ethical than involvement

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns about help that removes learning along with discomfort.
explanation.direct: Overhelping fits when it erases useful feedback and leaves the person less able to handle future strain independently.
explanation.competitive: The rescue feels kind now because it outsourced the future bill.

questions.prompt: What deeper shift does the chapter ask from the reader?
choices: Judge help by whether the surface looks smoother right away
Judge intervention by what it does to feedback, learning, and hidden fragility rather than by immediate calm alone
Assume that visible pain is better than calm in every case

explanation.gentle: The chapter changes the test from appearance to what the system can still learn.
explanation.direct: Taleb wants the reader to evaluate intervention by its effect on adaptive feedback and delayed fragility, not by short-term relief alone.
explanation.competitive: Stop grading the fix by how quiet the room gets and start grading it by what damage it is postponing or preventing.

questions.prompt: How does this chapter set up the move into prediction?
choices: It shows that systems can reward surface-level control even when they are losing contact with reality
It proves that forecasts replace intervention entirely
It argues that prediction is always a form of help

explanation.gentle: The next chapter asks why polished confidence keeps getting rewarded in systems already hiding fragility.
explanation.direct: The intervention critique prepares the prediction critique by showing how modern systems often prize neat appearances over real feedback from reality.
explanation.competitive: Once a system learns to love surface control, forecast prestige is the next costume that same mistake wears.
